In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of cytokine production during HIV‐1 infection.
the regulation of the type‐1 immune response in HIV‐inflected individuals.
the role of the CD4 molecule as a T‐cell surface receptor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CD40L expression in CD4 T lymphocytes of HIV+ individuals is reduced in a disease stage related fashion.
the CD40L‐CD40 interaction is an important mechanism in the regulation of type‐1 responses, and that this interaction is defective during HIV infection, contributing to the pathogenesis of AIDS.
HIV‐1 infection induces a profound dysregulation of the CD4+ T cell‐mediated immune response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HIV infection is associated with a defect in the CD40/CD40 ligand pathway, which may be a key factor contributing to the immune deficiency in AIDS patients.
HIV infection leads to a decrease in CD40L on CD4 T cell, and this decrease is correlated with the stage of the infection.
HIV‐1 infection leads to a dysregulated cytokine production, with an early increase of type 2 cytokines, followed by a deficiency of type 1 cytokines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV infection leads to dysregulation of the CD40–CD40L pathway, resulting in decreased CD40L expression on CD4 T helper cells and dysregulated expression of IL‐12.
CD40‐mediation of IL‐12 production is impaired in AIDS, but enhanced in early stages of HIV infection, and that this is due to defective CD40L expression on CD4 T lymphocytes.
